Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Apply explicit corrections to the final stated intent. Preserve meaningful filler-like words and unfinished thoughts. Apply clearly spoken punctuation and list cues. Keep the supplied language.", "input": "At the end of a rainy Tuesday, Mara Ellis brought the bakery’s new order form to the front counter and set it beside the register. The old form had been a photocopied sheet with narrow lines, and customers often ran out of room before they could describe a cake. Mara had drafted a replacement over the weekend, using notes from the counter staff and examples from recent orders. She wanted to see how it worked during an ordinary afternoon, so she asked Leon to use it for each new request and mark any confusing field in pencil.

The first customer, Mr. Okafor, ordered a lemon cake for his sister’s retirement gathering. He was not sure how many guests would attend, but he expected about eighteen people. The form asked for both the estimated serving count and the desired cake size, which helped Leon explain the difference without guessing what the customer meant. Mr. Okafor chose a two-layer cake and asked for a simple white finish with yellow flowers. In the space marked “Design or message,” Leon wrote the exact inscription the customer requested: “Congratulations, Ada!” He read it back before moving to the next section, and Mr. Okafor confirmed the spelling.

Mara watched as Leon filled in the date and pickup window. The form offered separate spaces for the event date and the day the order would be collected, since customers sometimes wanted to pick up a cake the day before a party. Mr. Okafor’s gathering was on Saturday, and he planned to collect the cake at 10:30 that morning. Leon copied the time onto the shop calendar and circled it on the customer’s copy. The form also included a telephone number field, with a note that staff could use the number only to clarify the order. Mr. Okafor supplied his mobile number and asked Leon to call after noon if a question came up, because he worked mornings at the library.

For the filling, he chose lemon curd between the layers. The form did not assume that a flavor choice also described an allergy, so Leon asked the separate question printed below the flavor list: “Are there any allergies or ingredients we should discuss before confirming this order?” Mr. Okafor said that his sister avoided almonds, although she had no diagnosed allergy. Leon recorded that statement in the allergy and ingredient notes field, using the customer’s wording rather than marking the order as nut-free. He explained that the bakery handled almonds in the kitchen and could not promise an environment without traces. Mr. Okafor said he understood and asked that the note remain visible to the decorating and packing staff.

Before taking payment, Leon turned the form around so Mr. Okafor could review the details. The price line was blank because the baker had not yet checked the requested size and decoration against that day’s price sheet. Rather than offer an estimate from memory, Leon wrote “price to be confirmed” in the staff section and pointed out that the order would not be entered as confirmed until the price had been discussed. Mr. Okafor was comfortable waiting. He left an email address and asked for a written quote, but he did not authorize a deposit at the counter. Leon checked the box labeled “Quote requested” and left the payment section untouched.

When the customer had gone, Mara examined the completed sheet. The handwriting was clear, and the design notes were long enough to describe the flowers without crowding the edges. She noticed that Leon had written the customer’s preferred call time in the notes rather than beside the telephone number. That seemed useful, because the phone field needed to remain easy to find while still making the timing visible to anyone following up. Mara added a small printed label, “Best time to call,” beneath the contact details on the next draft. She did not change the form during service; she wanted to keep the current copies consistent until the revised batch was ready.

1. Staff review before confirming an order:
   - Check the collection date and time against the shop calendar.
   - Read the inscription aloud and verify names and punctuation with the customer.
   - Review allergy or ingredient notes with the baker before making a promise about suitability.
   - Confirm the price and payment arrangement, then mark the order confirmed only after the customer agrees.

The list reflected what Leon had done, with one important distinction: asking for a quote was not the same as confirming an order. Mara kept the distinction in bold on the staff copy because the two boxes sat close together on the page. The baker, Nia, later checked the size and decoration against the price sheet and prepared a written quote. She called Mr. Okafor after noon, as requested, and explained that the cake could be made with the selected filling, but the bakery could not guarantee the absence of almond traces. He asked her to email the quote and said he would decide after speaking with his sister. Nia left the order marked “Quote sent,” not “Confirmed,” and did not reserve a production slot.

At closing, Mara placed the customer copy in the outgoing folder and filed the staff copy in the pending-orders tray. She attached the price sheet reference to the staff copy so the next person who opened it could see where the quote came from. The calendar entry remained provisional, written in pencil rather than ink. On the counter, the new form had held up through several other requests, including a dozen breakfast rolls and a small birthday tart.
